doc_name: List of Hot R&B Singles number ones of 1993
text: Billboard published a weekly chart in 1993 ranking the top-performing singles in the United States in African American-oriented genres; the chart has undergone various name changes over the decades to reflect the evolution of black music and has been published as Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs since 2005. In 1993, it was titled Hot R&B Singles, and 15 different singles reached number one. Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" broke several chart records that year; already number one for four weeks the previous year, it spent seven more weeks at number one, becoming the first single in the history of the R&B charts to block a new song from entering number one at the start of the year. With an eleven-week run at number one, it also broke the record for the longest-running number one single since Billboard merged its previously separate R&B sales and airplay charts in 1958. A number of acts topped the chart for the first time in 1993: Naughty by Nature, Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Silk, H-Town, SWV, Tag Team, Ice Cube, Das EFX, Xscape, and DRS. On the February 20, 1993, issue of Billboard, hip-hop group Naughty by Nature entered number one with "Hip Hop Hooray," which was replaced the following week by Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg with "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang," staying at the top for two weeks. The single was the lead track from Dr. Dre's solo debut album, The Chronic, which became one of the most important and influential albums of the 1990s and one of the best-produced hip-hop albums; in 2019, the Library of Congress selected it for preservation in the National Recording Registry as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant." Snoop Dogg later released his debut solo album, Doggystyle, which, like The Chronic, became one of the most significant albums of the 1990s and one of the most important hip-hop albums ever released; its distinctive sounds helped introduce the G-funk subgenre to a mainstream audience, establishing West Coast hip-hop as a dominant force in the early to mid-1990s. Snoop Dogg went on to sell over 23 million albums in the United States and 35 million worldwide. The Atlanta-based R&B group Silk's "Freak Me" topped the chart for nine straight weeks, the longest run of any act that year, from March 13 to May 1, with many of their early hits produced by Keith Sweat. The Houston-based group H-Town reached number one with "Knockin' Da Boots," which was replaced after four weeks by SWV's first number one single, "SWV," inspired by writer Brian Alexander Morgan's crush on R&B singer Chante Moore, spending two weeks at the top. Tag Team's "Whoomp! (There It Is)" then replaced that song at number one. Rapper Ice Cube achieved his first number one with "Check Yo Self," featuring the rap group Das EFX. On the October 16 issue, R&B group Xscape scored their first number one with Jermaine Dupri-produced "Just Kickin' It" for four weeks, before being replaced by DRS's "Gangsta Lean," which spent six weeks at number one from November 13 to December 18. SWV was the only act to have two number one singles that year. Four of the 1993 R&B number-ones also reached number one on Billboard's pop chart, the Hot 100.
